messages.subject: minor updates: new source() commands
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I've made a few minor updates, if you get one of these errors:

===========
Error in tipranges_to_tip_condlikes_of_data_on_each_state(tipranges, phy,  :
  unused argument (useAmbiguities = BioGeoBEARS_run_object$useAmbiguities)

or:

Error in check_BioGeoBEARS_run(BioGeoBEARS_run_object) :
  could not find function "geogtaxa"
===========

...it means you need to use the new source() commands in the example script:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#toc14
========
library(BioGeoBEARS)
source("http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--files/biogeobears/BioGeoBEARS_basics_v1.R")
source("http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--files/biogeobears/BioGeoBEARS_classes_v1.R")
source("http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--files/biogeobears/BioGeoBEARS_stratified_v1.R")
source("http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--files/biogeobears/BioGeoBEARS_models_v1.R")
source("http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--files/biogeobears/BioGeoBEARS_univ_model_v1.R")
source("http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--files/biogeobears/BioGeoBEARS_plots_v1.R")
source("http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--files/biogeobears/BioGeoBEARS_readwrite_v1.R")
source("http://phylo.wikidot.com/local--files/biogeobears/calc_loglike_sp_v01.R")
calc_loglike_sp = compiler::cmpfun(calc_loglike_sp_prebyte)    # crucial to fix bug in uppass calculations
========

...I've added another file or two since the last version of the example script, if their updates aren't sourced, you'll get those errors.

Cheers!
Nick

messages.subject: speed tests
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

As we all know, R is a slow language compared to Python or, especially, C++.  R has a lot of advantages in terms of graphics, the packages system, etc., but I've always been slightly sad that BioGeoBEARS wasn't as fast as C++ Lagrange (although, of course, BioGeoBEARS does more things).  For small problems, like the Psychotria dataset, C++ Lagrange is way faster, for the DEC model.

Well, I did design BioGeoBEARS to prioritize coping with the larger problems rather than the smaller ones.  I finally got around to doing a speed test on a dataset where BioGeoBEARS DEC should be faster than C++ Lagrange DEC.

This dataset has:

8 taxa, 10 areas, 6 max, for 848 states = 848 possible geographic ranges in the state space

transition matrix is 848x848 = 719,104 cells

number of (ancestor state, left descendant, right descendant) combinations to check at cladogenesis = 847*847*847 = 607,645,423

Here's the speed test on my computer (Intel Mac desktop, multicore)

BioGeoBEARS DEC w. single core = 187 minutes
BioGeoBEARS DEC w. 12 cores = 22 minutes
BioGeoBEARS DEC+J w. 12 cores = 81 minutes

Lagrange C++ DEC = 208 minutes
Lagrange Python DEC = couldn't get the Lagrange configurator website to take a problem with 10 areas

So, that multicore thing REALLY helps if you have a large state space.  I had kind of thought 848 states would be completely impractical, but it's doable.  It could probably be pushed somewhat further, especially if run on a cluster with hundreds of nodes.

Cheers!
Nick

messages.subject: CladoRcpp update (minor)
messages.body_plain:
I have done a minor update of CladoRcpp, which is now on CRAN:

http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/cladoRcpp/index.html

The changes do not affect the calculations, but you might as well update when you get a chance.  Binaries for various systems generally appear over the next few days.  The update appears first at CRAN 0-cloud and then spreads to the mirrors, so the best place to install from is repos="http://cran.rstudio.com":

install.packages("BioGeoBEARS", dependencies=TRUE, repos="http://cran.rstudio.com")

Cheers!
Nick

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] CladoRcpp update (minor)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ken, some thoughts/general wisdom

1. I think the changes to cladoRcpp are just propagating through the CRAN mirrors, which can take a day or two to build the binaries for everything.  Until then, you should be able to install from source:

install.packages("cladoRcpp", dependencies=TRUE, repos="http://cran.rstudio.com", type="source")
install.packages("BioGeoBEARS", dependencies=TRUE, repos="http://cran.rstudio.com", type="source")

...as the new (and old) source code is up:

http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/cladoRcpp/index.html
http://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/cladoRcpp/

http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/BioGeoBEARS/index.html
http://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/BioGeoBEARS/

Installing from source is usually, but not quite always, easy (Windows sometimes has issues).

2. If you have an R GUI of some sort, the menu option to install from source is something like (I'm using R.app on a Mac):

R menu bar --> Packages & Data --> Packages Installer --> change "CRAN (binaries)" to "CRAN (sources)" --> search on cladoRcpp --> click "Get List" --> pick package --> Click "Install selected"

3. You can also use either the command line or the menu to install a package when you have saved the source or binary on your local machine, just specify the file location.  The old source is always available on CRAN, sadly they don't seem to archive the binaries.

4. Regardless of all of the above, you should probably update to R 3.1, and there's a chance that will help.

5. You can track the online compilation of the packages for different systems via:

http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/cladoRcpp/index.html
http://cran.r-project.org/web/checks/check_results_cladoRcpp.html

http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/BioGeoBEARS/index.html
http://cran.r-project.org/web/checks/check_results_BioGeoBEARS.html

...as you can see, cladoRcpp 0.14.4 has not yet gone through all checks/systems yet.

6. Looking at http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/BioGeoBEARS/index.html , I see that one system has an issue with BioGeoBEARS because the package phylobase has an issue on that system.  Typically the solution would be to install an older version of phylobase (until the phylobase managers upgrade).  I will do a major update of BioGeoBEARS to try to remove all possible dependencies, they tend to cause cascading errors when some package maintainer goes on vacation or whatever.

7. If nothing works after checking the above, post the error message!

Cheers,
Nick

messages.subject: Manual states list / possible ranges list
messages.subject_clean: Manual states list / possible ranges list
messages.body_plain:
Just answered a question about having a manual list of states / possible ranges, rather than an auto-generated list based on number of areas and max_range_size.

This can be done and appears to work, although I have not extensively tested it.

# Basically, you would take the example script, and use these command to generate the default states_list:

areas = getareas_from_tipranges_object(tipranges)
tmp_states_list = rcpp_areas_list_to_states_list(areas=areas, maxareas=max_range_size, include_null_range=TRUE)

# Then, eliminate ranges of size=3 areas:

tmp_states_list_lengths = lapply(X=tmp_states_list, FUN=length)
tmp_states_list_lengths
TF = tmp_states_list_lengths == 3
tmp_states_list[TF] = NULL
tmp_states_list

# (you could also eliminate certain ranges by hand if you like)

# And store it in the run object:
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$states_list = tmp_states_list

...and run like normal.

It works in the default example, although I haven't tried every flavor of stratified analysis etc., so YMMV.

You do have to be careful to make sure that your transition matrix & cladogenesis matrix allow a probability above zero of your tip data!  E.g. a DEC model requires that AB be possible, if the tips are either A or B.

If you don't you'll get NaNs in the likelihood.  I've improved the error-checking a bit to at least flag where NaNs first appear:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#toc14

The manual ranges feature is one way to try and reduce the size of your state space to speed up calculation.  Often there are a lot of "weird" possible ranges that might not be realistic combinations of areas, if you remove them from the calculation, you will speed it up and also spread out your ancestral state probabilities over fewer options.

Cheers,
Nick

messages.subject: stochastic mapping in biogeography with BioGeoBEARS
messages.subject_clean: stochastic mapping in biogeography with BioGeoBEARS
messages.body_plain:
Hi again,

I've basically got working stochastic mapping functions for normal and stratified analyses now.  Basically you load in a results object containing an inferred model and it will output a table containing a realization/simulation of the possible history of events at nodes and along branches. By repeating this process many time, you can build up counts of different sorts of events, their timing, etc.

This should be a more objective way to test such hypotheses than the typical method people use in biogeography, which is squinting at the most-probable states at each node, interpreting this as a joint history (not really validly, although the amount of wrongness goes down as the precision of ancestral states goes up), and manually counting events they see.

These are simulations conditional on the inferred model and inferred ancestral state probabilities, and thus repeating them many times and averaging over the node states should produce the same probabilities at nodes as in the standard ancestral state inference.  What you don't get in standard inference is a sense of the variability in timing of events etc.

I am still working on documentation etc. (eventually for a major upgrade of BioGeoBEARS), and it may take awhile to get it finalized, but if anyone is dying to do stochastic mapping, email me.

Cheers!
Nick

messages.subject: understanding DEC vs. DIVALIKE
messages.body_plain:
This is an answer to a question about a dataset that has higher likelihood under DIVALIKE than under DEC.  The question was, what would explain this preference, and was it possibly due to DIVALIKE's ability to have widespread vicariance?  The analysis had a maximum range size of 2.

Cheers, Nick

Hi XXX,

If I understand you correctly, you have an analysis in which the maximum range size = 2 areas.

If this is the case, then DEC and DIVALIKE will be identical in how they treat vicariance.  Vicariance only differs between DEC and DIVALIKE when max_range_size >= 4, because only then is a split with the smaller daughter having 2 areas possible (i.e., you have 4 areas --> (2 areas, 2 areas)).

When max_range_size=2, the only difference between DEC and DIVALIKE is that DIVALIKE assigns a 0 weight to s, "subset sympatry".

Imagine if you had just 2 areas, A & B.  DEC would allow these cladogenesis events:

DEC cladogenesis events for 2 areas:

A->A,A (weight 1, conditional probability=1/1)
B->B,B (weight 1, conditional probability=1/1)
AB->A,AB (weight 1, conditional probability=1/6)
AB->B,AB (weight 1, conditional probability=1/6)
AB->AB,A (weight 1, conditional probability=1/6)
AB->AB,B (weight 1, conditional probability=1/6)
AB->A,B (weight 1, conditional probability=1/6)
AB->B,A (weight 1, conditional probability=1/6)

Whereas, for DIVALIKE with 2 areas:

A->A,A (weight 1, conditional probability=1/1)
B->B,B (weight 1, conditional probability=1/1)
AB->A,B (weight 1, conditional probability=1/2)
AB->B,A (weight 1, conditional probability=1/2)

If the subset sympatry events are not needed to explain your data, then they will reduce the likelihood (the probability of the data), because the probabilities will be spread out over more options.

So, e.g., if a 2-area dataset had lots of sister species with distributions like (A,B), I might expect DIVALIKE to beat DEC.  If the dataset had lots of sister species with distributions like (A, AB), I might expect DEC to beat DIVALIKE.

Cheers!
Nick

PS Note that the BioGeoBEARS DIVALIKE model is not identical to Ronquist's parsimony DIVA, rather, it is a likelihood interpretation of DIVA, where DIVA's processes are implemented in the way DEC implements those processes, modified to match DIVA's assumptions.
